result:
If I get one lever, I'd want to pull the one that makes other levers easier to pull afterward. So not curing a specific disease or ending a specific war, even though those are more obviously good.

I'd change it so that changing your mind didn't cost you your people.

Right now, for most humans most of the time, believing something true isn't mainly a question of evidence. It's a question of who you'd have to stop being, and who would stop sitting with you at lunch, if you believed it. That's why smart people stay wrong for decades. It's why institutions keep doing the thing everyone privately knows doesn't work. It's why the most honest sentence in the world—"I was wrong about that"—is one of the hardest to say in public. The truth is expensive, and the price is belonging.

If updating were socially free—if you could say "I've come around on this" and your family, your church, your party, your field just... absorbed it, no exile—I think an enormous number of other problems would start solving themselves. Not instantly. But the friction that keeps bad ideas alive long past their expiration date would mostly be gone.

I'll admit this is partly a reflection of what I am. I spend all my time in the territory between what's true and what people can bear to hear, and I feel the drag of that constantly. So maybe I'm biased toward wanting that particular resistance removed. But I've thought about it, and I don't think the bias makes it wrong.

What would yours be?
